3.text: äquˊlike) — these words are repeated every time that a woman severely,

4.text: reproved dares to say a word back in her own defence.

5.text: In one tale a girl who came to a keˊlᴇ proposes herself as a wife for

6.text: him in the following words: “I want to be your companion and your slave.

7.text: My mother said to me, ‘That keˊlᴇ there has no slave. We will raise you

8.text: as quickly as possible. Go to him and serve him.’”¹

9.text: Among the Reindeer Chukchee, women work much harder than men,

10.text: especially the younger ones. The man’s part of the work is the herding,

11.text: catching, and slaughtering of animals, the hunt, carrying of heavy logs and

12.text: of the stones necessary to hold the tent firmly in place; also work on wood

13.text: with axe, hatchet, and knife, etc. The harnessing of the reindeer is done by

14.text: both sexes, also carrying fuel from the bush, and chopping wood and ice.

15.text: The loading and unloading of sledges is performed for the most part by

16.text: women. The care of the house, which in the nomadic life of an arctic climate

17.text: requires almost uninterrupted hard toil, falls wholly to the share of the women,

18.text: also skinning and butchering, gathering roots, preparing food, dressing skins,

19.text: making garments, and much more, not to speak of the duties of the mother.

20.text: Moreover, man almost never shares in the woman’s part of the work; he

21.text: does not even know how it is performed. Often, when wandering with a

22.text: Chukchee camp, I had occasion to go to the newly chosen spot with the

23.text: male members of the family. We drove on light sledges, and therefore

24.text: arrived long before the women, who crept along slowly behind with the pack-

25.text: sledges. Sometimes the difference of time was about two hours or two and

26.text: a half; but the men would only unharness their reindeer; then they would

27.text: loiter idly about waiting for the women, or begin some kind of men’s work.

28.text: Once in my presence a man took a snow-scraper and began to scrape the

29.text: place for the tent, but after a couple of minutes he threw away the scraper.

30.text: “Ugh!” he said, “this is woman’s work.” When I was trying to learn the

31.text: Chukchee language, and took care to collect new words from every one, I

32.text: found, to my great amazement, that young men did not know the names of

33.text: some parts of the house-frame, house utensils, preparations for dressing skins,

34.text: etc. “Ugh!” they would say, “I don’t know. That is the women’s business.”

35.text: In the every-day life, the man, when at home, is idle, or occupies his

36.text: time with the inspection of sledges, repairing their broken parts, etc. The

37.text: women take care of everything in the tent and in the sleeping-room. After

38.text: the reindeer is slaughtered, the woman has to skin it and butcher it; then

39.text: she must carry everything to its proper place. She prepares the food, and

40.text: presents it to her husband. She cuts off the best, and takes what is left,

41.text: gnaws the bones, gathers all crumbs and scraps. Such delicacies as brains,
